281.quote_or_event: “I renounce all taking of anything not given, either in a village or a town or a wood, either of little or much, of small or great, of living or lifeless things.”
281.explanation: This is the opening of the third great vow (asteya) that every Jain monk takes. It renounces taking anything not given, whatever its size or value.
281.tie_back: Valluvar tells the man who wants to avoid contempt to guard his heart against taking “anything at all” by fraud. The Jain vow likewise allows no exception for small things: “of little or much, of small or great.”
281.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15, the third great vow (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 205-206)
281._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's translation on sacred-texts.com. It matches the Kural's 'nothing at all, however small' very closely, though the Kural's motive (avoiding contempt) is not part of the vow.

282.quote_or_event: “It follows that activity actuated by impure dispositions is stealing (steya), whether external objects are taken or not.”
282.explanation: Commenting on the sutra that defines stealing as taking what is not given, Pūjyapāda holds that the guilt lies in the passion (pramatta-yoga) behind the act. A theft-minded disposition is therefore already stealing, even if nothing is actually taken.
282.tie_back: Valluvar says that merely thinking “I will take his property by cunning” is already a wrong. Pūjyapāda likewise places stealing in the impure disposition itself, whether or not anything is taken.
282.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.15, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
282._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. It is a close doctrinal match for 'even the thought is evil'. This passage is also used for Kural 171 in this edition.

283.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
283.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained by evil means does not last. Its owners lose it and are left bound by their own passions.
283.tie_back: In the Kural, fraudulent wealth seems to swell but perishes and takes more with it. Here wealth acquired by evil deeds is lost and the acquirer is caught in further snares.
283._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Both texts say ill-gotten wealth is lost and leaves the owner worse off, though the Jain verse lacks the Kural's image of wealth seeming to grow.

284.quote_or_event: “Thus when he takes another's property, and is (after all) not satisfied by the 'colours' (he has obtained), he becomes unhappy, and nobody will protect him.”
284.explanation: Lecture 32 traces a chain: craving grows, greed leads a man to take another's property, and the theft brings only deeper misery and no protection. The lecture adds that passion accumulates karman, which in the end produces further misery.
284.tie_back: The Kural says an ingrained craving for fraudulent gain ripens into endless sorrow. The Jain text likewise shows craving that ends in theft bearing fruit only in unhappiness, with no one to protect the thief.
284._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong thematic fit (craving, then theft, then misery), but the passage is set within a lecture on sense-objects ('colours'), and 'endless' sorrow is only implied.

285.quote_or_event: “A thief feels neither pity nor shame, nor does he possess discipline and faith. There is no evil that he cannot do for wealth.”
285.explanation: Śivārya's Digambara manual on monastic discipline says that the thief's mind has no room for compassion. Its fixation on wealth crowds out pity, shame and faith.
285.tie_back: Valluvar says those who covet another's goods and wait for his careless moment cannot be people of compassion (aruḷ). The Jain verse says the same thing directly: “A thief feels neither pity nor shame.”
285.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 862 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
285._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com, an English rendering of a Digambara text that I did not check against the Prakrit. It closely matches the Kural's claim that the would-be defrauder lacks compassion.

286.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
286.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his kingdom, tells Indra that greed has no natural limit. No amount of wealth can satisfy it.
286.tie_back: The Kural says those in whom the love of fraudulent gain has hardened cannot keep within measure (aḷavu). Nami's verse describes the same measureless quality of greed, “boundless like space.”
286._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The verse is about greed in general, not fraud specifically, so it fits the 'no measure' theme only partly.

287.quote_or_event: “A Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should always take possession of a limited part of it and for a fixed time. The Kevalin says: If a Nirgrantha who has taken possession of some ground, should take possession of an unlimited part of it and for an unfixed time, he might take what is not given.”
287.explanation: One of the five clauses that protect the vow against stealing requires the monk to keep a strict limit on what he occupies and for how long. Going beyond that limit is treated as sliding into theft.
287.tie_back: Valluvar sets 'measure' (aḷavu) against the dark cleverness of fraud. The Jain clause makes the same link institutional: keeping to a fixed measure is what keeps one from taking what is not given.
287.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15, third great vow, third clause (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, p. 206)
287._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The link between measure and non-stealing is real, but the clause is a narrow monastic rule about lodging, while the Kural's aḷavu is a broader inner virtue.

288.quote_or_event: “When he is overcome by violent desire, takes another's property, and is not satisfied with those 'colours' and their possession, then his deceit and falsehood increase on account of his greed; yet he will not get rid of his misery.”
288.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes how one act of taking another's property leads to settled habits of deceit and falsehood, fed by greed.
288.tie_back: The Kural says deceit lives steadily in the hearts of those who have learned fraud. The Jain verse shows how deceit grows and takes root in the one who takes what belongs to others.
288._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It matches the 'deceit abides in the fraudster' half of the Kural, but has nothing parallel to the half about virtue abiding in those who know measure.

289.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
289.explanation: Jacobi's note gives the commentator Devendra's story. A burglar is caught by the feet in the hole he dug, and as his companion pulls him from the other side, the wall falls and crushes him: he dies in the very breach he made.
289.tie_back: Valluvar says those who know nothing but fraud are ruined 'right there' (āṅkē), in the act itself. The Jain image of the burglar killed in his own breach is almost exactly that picture.
289.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3, with Jacobi's note citing Devendra's commentary (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
289._accuracy_note: Verse and note both checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The image of a thief destroyed in the very act fits very closely. The detail of the wall falling comes from the medieval commentary that Jacobi summarises, not from the verse itself.

290.quote_or_event: “A sinner, though he be a mendicant (friar), will not escape hell; but a pious man, whether monk or householder, ascends to heaven.”
290.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon on two kinds of death says that destiny follows conduct, not status. Sinners fall to hell, while the virtuous, lay or monastic, rise to the heavens of the gods.
290.tie_back: The Kural closes the chapter by contrasting the fraudster, whom even bodily life fails, with the honest person, for whom the world of the gods does not fail. The Jain verse draws the same contrast between the sinner and the pious person who reaches heaven.
290._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The heaven-and-hell contrast fits, but the verse is about sin in general, not fraud, and in Jainism heaven is only a temporary birth short of liberation.
